entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sextus Placitus of Papyra, an ancient Roman physician, is best known for his Libri medicinae Sexti Placiti Papyriensis ex animalibus pecoribus et bestiis vel avibus Concordantiae. Born in the late 4th century CE, Placitus was a prominent figure in the medical community of the late Roman Empire. His work, which aimed to establish a systematic approach to animal anatomy, was widely influential among physicians and scholars of the time.

Placitus' contributions to medicine went beyond his written works, as he was also a skilled teacher and mentor. He trained many notable physicians, including the prominent physician and scholar, Aretaeus of Cappadocia. Through his teaching and research, Placitus helped shape the medical knowledge of the Roman Empire, leaving a lasting legacy in the field of anatomy and medicine.

Despite his significant contributions to medicine, Placitus' life and work remain somewhat shrouded in mystery. Little is known about his personal life, and his exact dates of birth and death are disputed among scholars. Nevertheless, his impact on the development of medical knowledge in the late Roman Empire is undeniable.

A testament to Placitus' enduring influence can be seen in the many works that built upon his ideas. The Roman physician and scholar, Galen of Pergamon, often credited Placitus as an inspiration for his own research and writings. This acknowledgement underscores the significant role Placitus played in shaping the medical landscape of the late Roman Empire.
